questions.title: Control of post-adenoidectomy bleeding
questions.question: Post adenoidectomy bleeding can be treated by:

explanations.A: Correct. The adenoid bed lies in the postnasal space, so bleeding after adenoidectomy is arrested by a posterior nasal (postnasal) pack that applies direct pressure to the nasopharynx. The pack is placed if simple measures fail and the child is kept under observation. Anterior packing alone does not reach the bleeding bed.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Local nasal steroids reduce mucosal inflammation over weeks and have no role in stopping active surgical haemorrhage.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Anti-inflammatory drugs do not control bleeding; some (like NSAIDs) can even worsen it by impairing platelet function.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A hydrogen peroxide mouth gargle cleans the oral cavity but cannot tamponade a bleeding nasopharyngeal adenoid bed.
explanations.E: Incorrect. There is an effective measure — a postnasal pack — so "none of the above" is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: State that post-adenoidectomy bleeding is controlled by a posterior (postnasal) pack.

questions.title: Effect not caused by adenoid enlargement
questions.question: Adenoid enlargement may result in any of the following EXCEPT:

options.C: High arched palate as a feature of adenoid facies.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Adenoid hypertrophy obstructs both Eustachian tube openings and causes bilateral secretory otitis media (middle ear effusion), so this is a genuine effect and not the exception.
explanations.B: Correct. Recurrent epistaxis is NOT a feature of adenoid enlargement; the adenoid is lymphoid tissue that obstructs and infects rather than bleeds. Nasal bleeding in this age group should instead raise suspicion of a vascular nasopharyngeal lesion such as juvenile angiofibroma. Every other listed effect follows directly from chronic nasopharyngeal obstruction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Chronic mouth breathing from adenoidal obstruction produces adenoid facies, of which a high-arched palate is a recognised part, so this is a true effect.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Nasopharyngeal obstruction causes snoring and obstructive sleep apnoea, a true and important effect of adenoid enlargement.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Eustachian tube obstruction and the adenoid acting as an infection reservoir cause recurrent acute otitis media, so this is a real effect.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that adenoid enlargement causes otitis media, adenoid facies and sleep apnoea but not epistaxis.

questions.title: Child with mouth breathing and hyponasality
questions.question: A 4 years old child presented by his mother complaining of lack of attention, mouth breathing and hyponasality:

explanations.A: Incorrect on its own. Secretory otitis media is indeed suspected (it explains the inattention through hearing loss), but option a is incomplete because the adenoid is the underlying cause and must also be suspected.
explanations.B: Incorrect on its own. Adenoid hypertrophy is suspected and explains the mouth breathing and hyponasal speech, but option b omits the associated secretory otitis media that explains the poor attention.
explanations.C: Correct. Adenoid hypertrophy causes mouth breathing and hyponasal (dead) speech by blocking the nasopharynx, and it simultaneously obstructs the Eustachian tubes to produce secretory otitis media, whose conductive hearing loss shows as inattention. Both diagnoses are therefore suspected together in this child. This is the classic adenoid symptom cluster.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The picture is a textbook presentation of adenoid hypertrophy with secretory otitis media, so "none of the above" is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: Link mouth breathing, hyponasality and inattention in a child to adenoid hypertrophy with secretory otitis media.

questions.title: Condition producing a high-arched palate
questions.question: Highly arched palate is found in cases of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Nasopharyngeal (juvenile) angiofibroma presents with epistaxis and obstruction in an adolescent male and does not produce the developmental facial changes of chronic childhood mouth breathing.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is a disease of adults presenting with a neck node, ear effusion and cranial nerve palsies, not a high-arched palate.
explanations.C: Correct. Long-standing adenoidal obstruction forces a child to mouth-breathe, and the resulting adenoid facies includes a high-arched (narrow) palate together with an open mouth, pinched nose and dull expression. The palate is remodelled because the tongue no longer rests against it during nasal breathing. This is why the high-arched palate is a marker of chronic adenoid hypertrophy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Allergic nasal polypi cause nasal obstruction and rhinorrhoea but are not classically associated with the high-arched palate of adenoid facies.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute the high-arched palate of adenoid facies to chronic adenoid hypertrophy.

questions.title: Commonest cause of bilateral nasal obstruction in a child
questions.question: The commonest cause of bilateral nasal obstruction in a child is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A deviated septum usually causes unilateral obstruction and is uncommon as a cause of bilateral blockage in a young child.
explanations.B: Correct. Adenoid hypertrophy is the commonest cause of bilateral nasal (nasopharyngeal) obstruction in children because the adenoid sits in the midline of the postnasal space and blocks both choanae. It presents with mouth breathing, hyponasal speech and snoring. This is why adenoidectomy is the usual remedy for the persistently blocked-nosed child.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Nasal polypi are uncommon in young children (and when present should prompt a search for cystic fibrosis), so they are not the commonest cause.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A nasal foreign body typically causes unilateral obstruction with a unilateral offensive discharge, not bilateral obstruction.

questions.learning_objective: Identify adenoid hypertrophy as the commonest cause of bilateral nasal obstruction in a child.

questions.title: False statement about nasopharyngeal carcinoma
questions.question: The following are true for nasopharyngeal carcinoma EXCEPT:

options.A: Radiotherapy is considered the treatment of choice.
options.B: It causes unilateral middle ear effusion.
options.C: The first cranial nerve to be affected is the facial nerve.
options.D: Sends metastases to the cervical lymph nodes.
options.E: The mass may extend into the nasal cavity.

explanations.A: Incorrect (true statement). Radiotherapy is the treatment of choice for nasopharyngeal carcinoma because the tumour is radiosensitive and surgically inaccessible, so this is true and not the exception.
explanations.B: Incorrect (true statement). The tumour obstructs one Eustachian tube and causes a unilateral middle ear effusion, a classic presenting sign, so this is true.
explanations.C: Correct (the false statement). The facial nerve is NOT the first cranial nerve affected; nasopharyngeal carcinoma spreads through the foramen lacerum to the cavernous sinus and typically involves the abducent (VI) nerve early, while the facial nerve is characteristically spared. Naming the facial nerve as the first affected is therefore the incorrect statement.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true statement). Nasopharyngeal carcinoma metastasises early to the cervical lymph nodes, so this is true.
explanations.E: Incorrect (true statement). The mass can extend anteriorly into the nasal cavity, so this is a genuine feature.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that the facial nerve is spared early in nasopharyngeal carcinoma while the abducent nerve is affected.

questions.title: Best investigation for nasopharyngeal angiofibroma
questions.question: The best investigation to diagnose nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is:

explanations.A: Incorrect and dangerous. Biopsy of a juvenile angiofibroma is contraindicated because the lesion is extremely vascular and biopsy can provoke torrential, life-threatening haemorrhage.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A plain x-ray cannot characterise a vascular soft-tissue nasopharyngeal mass or define its feeding vessels.
explanations.C: Correct. Carotid (or the more specific external carotid) angiography demonstrates the characteristic tumour blush and identifies the feeding vessels of a juvenile angiofibroma, and it is therapeutic as well because the feeders can be embolised before surgery. Contrast CT/MRI provide anatomical extent, but among the options angiography is the definitive vascular investigation. Crucially it lets the diagnosis be made without a hazardous biopsy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ultrasonography does not image a deep nasopharyngeal mass or its skull-base extension adequately.

questions.learning_objective: State that juvenile angiofibroma is investigated by angiography (with embolisation) and that biopsy is contraindicated.

questions.title: Commonest presentation of nasopharyngeal carcinoma
questions.question: Most common presentation in nasopharyngeal carcinoma:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Blood-stained nasal discharge can occur, but frank epistaxis is not the commonest presenting complaint of nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hoarseness is a laryngeal symptom and is not typical of nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Nasal stuffiness may occur once the tumour is bulky but is not the usual first presentation.
explanations.D: Correct. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma most often presents as a painless cervical lymph node mass, because it metastasises early to the upper deep cervical (and posterior triangle) nodes. Many patients seek advice for the neck swelling before any nasal or aural symptom. This is why an adult with an unexplained upper neck node warrants nasopharyngeal examination.

questions.learning_objective: State that the commonest presentation of nasopharyngeal carcinoma is a cervical lymph node mass.

questions.title: First step for an adolescent with a vascular nasal mass
questions.question: A 15 years old boy presented with history of recurrent epistaxis and protrusion of the eye ball that started one year ago. On examination there was a unilateral fleshy nasal mass on the side of the proptosis. The first important step to do is to:

options.A: Schedule the patient for urgent surgery to remove the mass.
options.B: Do CT of the nose and paranasal sinuses and angiography if found to be vascular.
options.C: Take biopsy from the mass to reach a histological diagnosis.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Rushing to surgery without imaging and preoperative embolisation risks massive intra-operative haemorrhage in a vascular tumour.
explanations.B: Correct. An adolescent male with recurrent epistaxis, proptosis and a fleshy nasal mass has a juvenile angiofibroma until proven otherwise, so the first step is contrast CT of the nose and paranasal sinuses to map extent, followed by angiography if the mass is vascular. Angiography both confirms the vascular nature and allows preoperative embolisation. This imaging-first pathway deliberately avoids an office biopsy.
explanations.C: Incorrect and dangerous. Biopsy of a suspected angiofibroma can cause severe uncontrolled bleeding and is contraindicated.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Antibiotics and analgesics do not address a vascular nasopharyngeal tumour and would delay diagnosis.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Local steroids treat inflammatory/allergic mucosal disease, not an angiofibroma.

questions.learning_objective: Choose CT plus angiography (not biopsy) as the first step for a suspected juvenile angiofibroma.

questions.title: Diagnosis of an enhancing nasopharyngeal mass in a boy
questions.question: A 15 year old male with blood stained nasal discharge and conductive deafness. Examination revealed large nasopharyngeal mass. CT showed an enhancing mass in the nasopharynx. The most likely diagnosis is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is a tumour of adults; it would be very unusual at 15 years, and it does not characteristically show the intense vascular enhancement seen here.
explanations.B: Correct. A 15-year-old male with blood-stained nasal discharge, conductive deafness (Eustachian tube obstruction) and a strongly enhancing nasopharyngeal mass on CT is the classic picture of juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma, a highly vascular benign tumour of adolescent boys. The avid contrast enhancement reflects its vascularity. Age, sex, epistaxis and the enhancing mass together point to angiofibroma.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Rhinoscleroma is a chronic granulomatous infection of the nose, not a solitary enhancing nasopharyngeal mass in a teenager.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Maxillary sinus carcinoma arises in the antrum of older adults and presents with cheek/alveolar signs, not a nasopharyngeal mass in a boy.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Inverted papilloma arises from the lateral nasal wall in adults and is not typically an enhancing nasopharyngeal mass in an adolescent.

questions.learning_objective: Diagnose juvenile angiofibroma from an adolescent male with epistaxis and an enhancing nasopharyngeal mass.

questions.title: False statement about nasopharyngeal angiofibroma
questions.question: All the following about nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is true EXCEPT:

options.B: epistaxis and nasal obstruction are common
options.C: radiotherapy is the treatment of choice

explanations.A: Incorrect (true statement). Juvenile angiofibroma occurs almost exclusively in adolescent males, so this is true and not the exception.
explanations.B: Incorrect (true statement). Recurrent severe epistaxis and progressive nasal obstruction are the common presenting features, so this is true.
explanations.C: Correct (the false statement). Radiotherapy is NOT the treatment of choice; juvenile angiofibroma is treated by surgical excision after preoperative embolisation, with radiotherapy reserved for inaccessible intracranial extension. Because it is a benign vascular tumour, surgery is curative and irradiating a child is avoided. Naming radiotherapy as the treatment of choice is therefore incorrect.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true statement). The tumour arises at the sphenopalatine foramen region of the posterolateral nasopharynx, so this is a true statement.

questions.learning_objective: State that juvenile angiofibroma is treated by surgical excision, not radiotherapy.

questions.title: Cranial nerve spared in nasopharyngeal carcinoma
questions.question: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma can cause paralysis of the following nerves EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The vagus can be paralysed when the tumour reaches the jugular foramen/parapharyngeal space, so it is not the exception.
explanations.B: Correct. The facial nerve is characteristically spared in nasopharyngeal carcinoma because it runs within the temporal bone away from the tumour's route of spread. The carcinoma instead reaches the cavernous sinus (affecting III, IV, V, VI, with the abducent often first) and the jugular foramen (affecting IX, X, XI, XII). The facial nerve is therefore the nerve NOT paralysed.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The glossopharyngeal nerve can be involved at the jugular foramen, so it is not the exception.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The abducent nerve is often the first affected as the tumour invades the cavernous sinus, so it is not the exception.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that the facial nerve is spared while the abducent, vagus and glossopharyngeal nerves can be paralysed in nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

questions.title: Treatment of choice in nasopharyngeal carcinoma
questions.question: Treatment of choice in nasopharyngeal carcinoma is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The nasopharynx is surgically inaccessible and the tumour spreads submucosally and to nodes, so surgery is not the primary treatment.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Chemotherapy is used as an adjuvant (concurrent chemoradiation) for advanced disease but is not the treatment of choice on its own.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Immunotherapy is not the standard first-line treatment for nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
explanations.D: Correct. Radiotherapy is the treatment of choice for nasopharyngeal carcinoma because the tumour is radiosensitive and its site precludes surgical clearance, and the bilateral neck nodes are included in the field. Chemotherapy is added concurrently for advanced tumours. This is why radiotherapy, not surgery, anchors management.

questions.learning_objective: State that radiotherapy is the treatment of choice for nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

questions.title: Age and sex affected by nasopharyngeal angiofibroma
questions.question: Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma affects only:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Angiofibroma is not a tumour of infants; it appears around puberty.
explanations.B: Correct. Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma affects almost exclusively young (adolescent) males, typically between about 10 and 20 years of age. Its striking sex restriction is a defining feature and reflects a hormone-related growth. This is why the same vascular tumour is essentially never seen in girls or older adults.
explanations.C: Incorrect. It is essentially not seen in females, so "adolescent females" is wrong.
explanations.D: Incorrect. It presents in adolescence rather than adulthood, and lesions often involute after growth ceases.
explanations.E: Incorrect. It is a tumour of the young, not the elderly.

questions.learning_objective: State that juvenile angiofibroma occurs almost exclusively in adolescent males.

questions.title: Complications of acute tonsillitis
questions.question: Complications of acute tonsillitis include:

explanations.A: Incorrect on its own. Rheumatic fever is a real non-suppurative complication of a group A streptococcal throat, but it is not the only complication listed.
explanations.B: Incorrect on its own. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is another recognised non-suppurative complication, but again it is not the complete answer.
explanations.C: Incorrect on its own. Quinsy (peritonsillar abscess) is the classic suppurative complication, yet it is only one of the three correct items.
explanations.D: Correct. Acute (streptococcal) tonsillitis can be complicated by suppurative spread such as quinsy and by the non-suppurative sequelae rheumatic fever and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. Because all three listed items are genuine complications, "all of the above" is the correct choice. This breadth is why streptococcal tonsillitis is treated with a full antibiotic course.

questions.learning_objective: List rheumatic fever, glomerulonephritis and quinsy as complications of acute tonsillitis.

questions.title: Cause of secondary post-tonsillectomy bleeding
questions.question: The main cause of secondary post tonsillectomy bleeding is:

options.B: Slipped ligature in the tonsillar bed.
options.D: Infection at the site of the operation.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Elevated blood pressure or a slipped ligature causes early (reactionary/primary) bleeding within the first hours, not the delayed secondary bleed.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A slipped ligature produces reactionary haemorrhage within the first 24 hours, whereas secondary bleeding comes days later.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A coagulation defect tends to cause immediate/primary bleeding and would usually be evident at operation, not as an isolated secondary bleed.
explanations.D: Correct. Secondary (delayed) post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage occurs around the fifth to tenth day and is caused by infection of the tonsillar bed that separates the healing slough and erodes a vessel. It is therefore managed with antibiotics and supportive measures, with surgery reserved for heavy bleeding. Infection, not a technical or clotting fault, is the main cause of the late bleed.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute secondary post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage to infection of the tonsillar bed.

questions.title: Indications of tonsillectomy
questions.question: Indications of tonsillectomy are:

options.B: Tonsillar hypertrophy causing obstructive sleep apnea.

explanations.A: Incorrect on its own. Recurrent acute tonsillitis is a leading indication, but it is not the only listed one.
explanations.B: Incorrect on its own. Obstructive tonsillar hypertrophy causing sleep apnoea is a strong indication, yet only part of the answer.
explanations.C: Incorrect on its own. A previous quinsy (peritonsillar abscess) is an accepted indication for interval tonsillectomy, but not the complete answer.
explanations.D: Incorrect on its own. Tonsillitis-related rheumatic fever or glomerulonephritis justifies removing the focus, but this is still only one of the listed indications.
explanations.E: Correct. Tonsillectomy is indicated for recurrent acute tonsillitis, obstructive hypertrophy causing sleep apnoea, a previous quinsy, and when the tonsils are the focus for rheumatic fever or glomerulonephritis. Since every listed item is a genuine indication, "all of the above" is correct. These indications are why the operation remains common in children and young adults.

questions.learning_objective: List the indications for tonsillectomy: recurrent tonsillitis, obstructive hypertrophy, quinsy and a rheumatic/nephritic focus.

questions.title: Timing of secondary post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage
questions.question: Secondary haemorrhage after tonsillectomy is most commonly seen:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Bleeding during surgery is primary haemorrhage, not secondary.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Bleeding immediately after surgery is reactionary haemorrhage occurring within the first 24 hours.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Bleeding at 24 hours still falls within the reactionary window rather than the delayed secondary one.
explanations.D: Correct. Secondary post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage most commonly occurs around the sixth day (within the fifth-to-tenth-day window), when infection separates the healing slough over the tonsillar bed. The timing reflects the peak of local sepsis after surgery. Recognising this window guides parents to expect and report a late bleed.
explanations.E: Incorrect. By four weeks the tonsillar fossa has healed, so bleeding this late is not the usual secondary haemorrhage.

questions.learning_objective: State that secondary post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage typically occurs around the sixth day after surgery.

questions.title: Management of secondary post-tonsillectomy bleeding
questions.question: A 5-year-old boy presented to the emergency room with bleeding from the mouth. He underwent tonsillectomy one week ago. His surgery went uneventful and he was discharged home the same day in a stable condition. Six days later, he started to spit a few blood drops. Then, bleeding gradually progressed. His haemoglobin on admission was 11.5. Management of such a case should be:

options.A: Surgical intervention in the form of ligation of the bleeders.
options.B: Admission to the hospital, observation and IV antibiotics.
options.C: Immediate tracheostomy to save his airway.
options.D: Immediate blood transfusion to replace his blood loss.
options.E: Angiography and embolization of the bleeding vessels.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Surgical ligation is reserved for a heavy or continuing secondary bleed; a minor day-six bleed with a stable haemoglobin of 11.5 does not need theatre first.
explanations.B: Correct. This is a secondary post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage, beginning about the sixth day when infection separates the slough over the tonsillar bed. A stable child with only a small bleed and a near-normal haemoglobin is managed by admission, observation, rehydration and intravenous antibiotics to treat the underlying infection. Surgical ligation is held in reserve for bleeding that is heavy or does not settle.
explanations.C: Incorrect. There is no airway compromise, so an immediate tracheostomy is unwarranted and would add serious morbidity.
explanations.D: Incorrect. With a haemoglobin of 11.5 and a small bleed, immediate transfusion is not indicated; transfusion is guided by the actual volume of blood loss, not given reflexively.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Angiography and embolisation are used for uncontrollable arterial bleeding, not for a minor infective secondary bleed that responds to antibiotics and observation.

questions.learning_objective: Manage a stable secondary post-tonsillectomy bleed with admission, observation and IV antibiotics.

questions.title: Absolute contraindication to tonsillectomy
questions.question: Tonsillectomy is absolutely contraindicated in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Chronic tonsillitis is an indication for tonsillectomy, not a contraindication.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A previous quinsy is in fact an accepted indication for interval tonsillectomy; an active quinsy only delays surgery, it is not an absolute bar.
explanations.C: Correct. An uncorrected bleeding disorder such as haemophilia is an absolute contraindication to tonsillectomy, because the raw tonsillar bed cannot be reliably controlled and fatal haemorrhage may follow. The coagulopathy must be corrected before any consideration of surgery. This is why a bleeding history is screened for before the operation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Age below five is not an absolute contraindication; tonsillectomy is done in younger children when clearly indicated, such as for obstructive sleep apnoea, with appropriate care.

questions.learning_objective: Identify an uncorrected bleeding disorder as the absolute contraindication to tonsillectomy.

questions.title: False statement about acute tonsillitis
questions.question: The following is not true about acute tonsillitis:

options.A: It is more common in children.
options.B: It may be complicated by rheumatic fever.
options.C: Complete blood count shows marked eosinophilia.
options.D: Is accompanied by enlarged tender jugulo-digastric lymph nodes.

explanations.A: Incorrect (true statement). Acute tonsillitis is indeed more common in children, so this is true and not the exception.
explanations.B: Incorrect (true statement). Streptococcal tonsillitis may be complicated by rheumatic fever, so this is true.
explanations.C: Correct (the false statement). Acute tonsillitis is a bacterial infection and its complete blood count shows a neutrophil leucocytosis, not marked eosinophilia. Eosinophilia points instead to allergic or parasitic disease. Naming marked eosinophilia as a feature is therefore the untrue statement.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true statement). The jugulodigastric (tonsillar) lymph nodes become enlarged and tender in acute tonsillitis, so this is true.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that acute tonsillitis shows a neutrophil leucocytosis, not eosinophilia.

questions.title: Timing of primary haemorrhage in tonsillectomy
questions.question: Primary haemorrhage in tonsillectomy occurs:

options.A: Within the first 24 hours following the operation.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Bleeding within the first 24 hours is reactionary haemorrhage, not primary.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Bleeding after one week is secondary haemorrhage, from infection of the tonsillar bed.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Bleeding within two days falls in the reactionary or early secondary window, not the primary one.
explanations.D: Correct. Primary haemorrhage is the bleeding that occurs during the operation itself, as the tonsil is removed and the bed is raw. It is controlled at the time by pressure, ligation or diathermy. Reactionary bleeding (first 24 hours) and secondary bleeding (fifth to tenth day) are the later categories.

questions.learning_objective: State that primary haemorrhage in tonsillectomy occurs during the operation.

questions.title: Timing of reactionary haemorrhage
questions.question: Reactionary hemorrhage occurs:

options.B: Within the first day after the operation.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Bleeding during the operation is primary haemorrhage, not reactionary.
explanations.B: Correct. Reactionary haemorrhage occurs within the first 24 hours (the first day) after the operation, typically from a slipped ligature or a rise in blood pressure as the patient recovers from anaesthesia. It is distinct from primary bleeding during surgery and from the later secondary bleed. Recognising this early window prompts prompt re-examination and control.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Bleeding from two to five days is drifting toward the secondary window rather than the reactionary one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Bleeding from five to fifteen days is secondary haemorrhage, caused by infection of the healing bed.

questions.learning_objective: State that reactionary post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage occurs within the first 24 hours.

questions.title: Not an indication for tonsillectomy
questions.question: Indications of tonsillectomy include the following except:

options.A: Repeated attacks of tonsillitis more than 5 attacks per year.
options.B: Single attack of acute follicular tonsillitis with very high fever.

explanations.A: Incorrect (true indication). Recurrent tonsillitis with more than about five attacks per year is a classic indication, so it is not the exception.
explanations.B: Correct (the exception). A single attack of acute follicular tonsillitis, however high the fever, is not an indication for tonsillectomy; the operation is reserved for recurrent or complicated disease. One episode is treated medically. Naming a single attack as an indication is therefore the incorrect option.
explanations.C: Incorrect (true indication). A previous quinsy (peritonsillar abscess) is an accepted indication for interval tonsillectomy, so it is not the exception.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true indication). Tonsillar hypertrophy causing obstructive sleep apnoea is a strong indication for tonsillectomy, so it is not the exception.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that a single attack of tonsillitis is not an indication for tonsillectomy.

questions.title: Multiple oral ulcers in a healthy young adult
questions.question: A 30 year old female, otherwise healthy, presented with odynophagia of few days duration. On examination of the oral cavity, multiple ulcers were seen in the soft palate, inner cheeks and oropharyngeal walls. The most probable pathogenesis of such ulcers is:

explanations.A: Correct. Multiple painful ulcers on the soft palate, inner cheeks and oropharyngeal walls of an otherwise healthy young adult are typical recurrent aphthous ulcers. They are multiple, recurrent and self-limiting, healing within one to two weeks. This benign pattern fits the picture far better than a neoplastic or infective membrane.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Leukoplakia is a white plaque rather than multiple painful ulcers, and is a disease of older smokers.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Diphtheria produces a single adherent membrane with systemic toxaemia, not scattered multiple ulcers in a well patient.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Carcinoma in situ presents as a solitary persistent lesion in an older or high-risk patient, not multiple acute ulcers in a healthy 30-year-old.

questions.learning_objective: Diagnose multiple recurrent oral ulcers in a healthy young adult as aphthous ulcers.

questions.title: Condition producing a true pharyngeal membrane
questions.question: A true membrane occurs on the pharyngeal mucosa in:

explanations.A: Correct. A true membrane — greyish, firmly adherent, bleeding when peeled off and reforming — occurs in diphtheria. It reflects mucosal necrosis produced by the diphtheria toxin. This is the classic sign that separates diphtheria from other causes of pharyngeal exudate.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Acute follicular tonsillitis gives a false membrane of exudate over the crypts that wipes off without bleeding.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Vincent's angina produces an ulcer with a greyish slough rather than a true adherent bleeding membrane.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Infectious mononucleosis causes a whitish exudate on enlarged tonsils that is not a true membrane.

questions.learning_objective: State that a true pharyngeal membrane occurs in diphtheria.

questions.title: False statement about oral moniliasis
questions.question: In oral moniliasis all is true except:

options.A: Presents by whitish patches in the oropharynx.
options.B: Is treated by massive doses of antibiotics.

explanations.A: Incorrect (true statement). Oral moniliasis presents with removable whitish patches in the oropharynx, so this is true.
explanations.B: Correct (the false statement). Oral moniliasis is a fungal (candidal) infection and is treated with antifungals such as nystatin, not antibiotics. Massive doses of antibiotics do not help and actually worsen it by suppressing the competing normal flora. Naming antibiotics as the treatment is therefore the untrue statement.
explanations.C: Incorrect (true statement). Moniliasis is common in immunocompromised and debilitated patients, so this is true.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true statement). Oral moniliasis is caused by Candida albicans, so this is true.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that oral moniliasis is candidal and is treated with antifungals, not antibiotics.

questions.title: Causes of oropharyngeal ulcers
questions.question: Oropharyngeal ulcers can be due to:

explanations.A: Incorrect on its own. Mechanical trauma from a sharp tooth or denture is a genuine cause, but it is not the only one listed.
explanations.B: Incorrect on its own. Herpes simplex is a real viral cause of oropharyngeal ulceration, but only one of several correct items.
explanations.C: Incorrect on its own. Dyspepsia and reflux can ulcerate the oropharyngeal mucosa, yet this is still only part of the answer.
explanations.D: Incorrect on its own. Agranulocytosis is a recognised haematological cause of oropharyngeal ulcers, but again not the complete answer.
explanations.E: Correct. Oropharyngeal ulcers have a broad differential, and mechanical trauma, herpes simplex, dyspepsia and agranulocytosis are each genuine causes. Because all four listed items are true causes, all of the above is the correct choice. This breadth is why an oropharyngeal ulcer prompts a search across traumatic, infective, dyspeptic and haematological groups.

questions.learning_objective: List trauma, herpes simplex, dyspepsia and agranulocytosis as causes of oropharyngeal ulcers.
questions.author_notes: Source printed six options a-f; the redundant never-correct filler f) 'None of the above' was dropped to fit the 4-5 option contract, keeping e) 'All of the above' as the printed key (grid key e).

questions.title: False statement about aphthous ulceration
questions.question: Apthous ulceration of the pharynx is characterized by the following except:

explanations.A: Incorrect (true statement). Aphthous ulcers are recurrent, so this is a genuine feature and not the exception.
explanations.B: Incorrect (true statement). They are typically multiple, so this is true.
explanations.C: Incorrect (true statement). Aphthous ulcers heal spontaneously within one to two weeks, so this is true.
explanations.D: Correct (the false statement). Aphthous ulcers are not caused by a fungus; their cause is idiopathic and multifactorial, and candidal disease is a separate entity. Because a fungal cause is untrue, this is the exception. The other three features — recurrent, multiple and self-limiting — are all genuine.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that aphthous ulcers are recurrent, multiple and self-limiting, and are not fungal.

questions.title: Site of pus in Ludwig's angina
questions.question: Accumulation of pus in Ludwig's angina occurs in the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The parapharyngeal (lateral pharyngeal) space is a different deep-neck space, not the seat of Ludwig's angina.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The retropharyngeal space lies behind the pharynx and is not where Ludwig's angina collects.
explanations.C: Correct. Ludwig's angina is a cellulitis of the submandibular space, usually from a lower molar dental infection, in which oedema and pus elevate the floor of the mouth and the tongue and threaten the airway. The collection is submandibular. This is why airway vigilance and dental source control are central to its management.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The prevertebral space lies in front of the vertebrae and is not involved in Ludwig's angina.

questions.learning_objective: State that Ludwig's angina collects in the submandibular space.

questions.title: Feature not part of a parapharyngeal abscess
questions.question: "Beck's Triad" include all of the following EXCEPT:

options.A: Swelling in the lateral pharyngeal wall pushing a normal tonsil medially.
options.B: Tender firm external swelling in the lateral side of the neck.
options.D: White spots on the surface of the tonsil.

explanations.A: Incorrect (a true feature). Swelling of the lateral pharyngeal wall pushing a normal tonsil medially is a sign of a parapharyngeal (lateral pharyngeal) abscess, so it is not the exception.
explanations.B: Incorrect (a true feature). A tender firm external swelling on the lateral side of the neck is part of the parapharyngeal abscess picture, so it is not the exception.
explanations.C: Incorrect (a true feature). Trismus from pterygoid irritation accompanies a parapharyngeal abscess, so it is not the exception.
explanations.D: Correct (the exception). White spots on the tonsil surface are a sign of tonsillitis, not of a parapharyngeal (lateral pharyngeal) space abscess. The abscess is characterised by a medially displaced normal tonsil, an external neck swelling and trismus. White spots on the tonsil therefore do not belong with the deep-space signs.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that white spots on the tonsil are not part of a parapharyngeal abscess, whose signs are a displaced tonsil, external neck swelling and trismus.

questions.title: Initial treatment of quinsy
questions.question: A 20-year-old male presented to the Emergency Room complaining of severe throbbing pain in the right side of his throat. His pain started two days ago and rapidly progressed and became throbbing in nature. On examination, his temperature was 38. He could not open his mouth properly during oral examination. The palate was found to be swollen and the tonsil was pushed medially and downwards. His upper deep cervical nodes were enlarged and tender. The initial line of treatment is:

options.B: Incision and Drainage under Local Anesthesia.
options.C: CT scan to diagnose the extension of the disease.
options.E: Tracheostomy to avoid any airway compromise.

explanations.A: Correct. This is a quinsy (peritonsillar abscess). The initial line of treatment is intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics, together with rehydration and analgesia, to control the infection and settle a peritonsillar cellulitis. Incision and drainage follows if frank pus has formed or there is no response. Starting with antibiotics is therefore the correct first step.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Incision and drainage is the step reserved for frank pus or failure of antibiotics, not the initial blanket treatment.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The diagnosis of quinsy is clinical, so a CT scan is not the initial step in this straightforward presentation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Intravenous fluids are only supportive; they do not treat the infection and are not the definitive initial line.
explanations.E: Incorrect. There is no airway compromise, so a tracheostomy is not indicated.

questions.learning_objective: Choose intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics as the initial treatment of quinsy, with drainage reserved for frank pus or non-response.

questions.title: Space not a site of head and neck abscess
questions.question: The following spaces can be the site of "abscess formation" in the area of the head and neck EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The peritonsillar space is the site of a quinsy, a genuine deep neck abscess, so it is not the exception.
explanations.B: Correct (the exception). The paraglottic space is an internal laryngeal space involved in the spread of laryngeal cancer, not a site of deep neck abscess. The true deep-neck abscess spaces are the peritonsillar, parapharyngeal, retropharyngeal and submandibular spaces. Naming the paraglottic space as an abscess site is therefore the exception.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The parapharyngeal space is a recognised deep neck abscess site, so it is not the exception.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The retropharyngeal space is a recognised deep neck abscess site, so it is not the exception.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The submandibular space is the site of Ludwig's angina, so it is not the exception.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that the paraglottic space is not a deep neck abscess site.

questions.title: Definition of quinsy
questions.question: Quinsy means collection of pus in the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The parapharyngeal space is a separate deep-neck space, not the seat of a quinsy.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The retropharyngeal space lies behind the pharynx and is not where a quinsy collects.
explanations.C: Correct. Quinsy is a peritonsillar abscess: a collection of pus between the tonsillar capsule and the superior constrictor muscle, in the peritonsillar space. It usually complicates acute tonsillitis and pushes the tonsil medially. The peritonsillar location is the definition.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Crypto magna" is not a deep-neck space; the crypta magna is a tonsillar crypt, not the site of a quinsy.

questions.learning_objective: State that quinsy is a collection of pus in the peritonsillar space.

questions.title: Relief of a quinsy not responding to antibiotics
questions.question: A 20 years old man c/o fever & increasing sore throat with dripping of saliva & trismus for only 2 days on examination (the right tonsil pushed medially & forward) no response to antibiotics.. rapid relief can be obtained by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Radiotherapy has no role in an acute peritonsillar abscess.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Reassurance and rest will not relieve a collection of pus that has failed to respond to antibiotics.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Antidiphtheritic serum treats diphtheria, not a quinsy.
explanations.D: Correct. This is a quinsy (peritonsillar abscess) that has not responded to antibiotics, so rapid relief is obtained by incision and drainage (or needle aspiration) of the pus. Draining the abscess relieves the pain, trismus and dysphagia at once. Drainage is the definitive step once pus has formed or antibiotics have failed.

questions.learning_objective: State that a quinsy not responding to antibiotics is relieved by incision and drainage.

questions.title: Feature not seen in acute retropharyngeal abscess
questions.question: Acute retropharyngeal abscess presents by the following except:

options.C: A swelling in the posterior pharyngeal wall.

explanations.A: Incorrect (a true feature). Fever, malaise and anorexia accompany an acute retropharyngeal abscess, so this is not the exception.
explanations.B: Incorrect (a true feature). Dysphagia and odynophagia are typical, so this is not the exception.
explanations.C: Incorrect (a true feature). A bulging swelling of the posterior pharyngeal wall is the local sign, so this is not the exception.
explanations.D: Correct (the exception). Trismus is not a feature of a retropharyngeal abscess, because the pterygoid muscles are not involved; trismus instead points to a peritonsillar or parapharyngeal collection. The retropharyngeal abscess gives fever, dysphagia and a posterior wall swelling without trismus. Naming trismus as a feature is therefore the exception.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that trismus is not a feature of an acute retropharyngeal abscess.

questions.title: Age group affected by acute retropharyngeal abscess
questions.question: Acute retropharyngeal abscess affects mainly:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The elderly are not the main group; the responsible retropharyngeal nodes have long since atrophied.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Adult males are not the main group affected by the acute abscess.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Adult females are not the main group affected.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Adolescents are not the typical group; the nodes atrophy before this age.
explanations.E: Correct. Acute retropharyngeal abscess affects mainly infants and young children, in whom prominent retropharyngeal lymph nodes suppurate after an upper respiratory infection. These nodes atrophy with age, so the acute abscess is uncommon later in life. Age is therefore a key pointer to the diagnosis.

questions.learning_objective: State that acute retropharyngeal abscess affects mainly infants and young children.

questions.title: False statement about quinsy symptoms
questions.question: Choose the false answer regarding Quinsy symptoms:

explanations.A: Incorrect (a true symptom). Severe dysphagia is characteristic of quinsy, so it is not the false answer.
explanations.B: Correct (the false statement). Hoarseness of voice is a laryngeal symptom and is not a feature of quinsy; quinsy instead gives a muffled hot-potato voice. Listing hoarseness among quinsy symptoms is therefore false. The genuine symptoms are dysphagia, trismus and dribbling of saliva.
explanations.C: Incorrect (a true symptom). Trismus from pterygoid irritation is typical of quinsy, so it is not the false answer.
explanations.D: Incorrect (a true symptom). Dribbling of saliva from painful swallowing is characteristic of quinsy, so it is not the false answer.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that hoarseness is not a symptom of quinsy.
